analysis.one_liner: Repealed the capital gains tax, cut top income tax rates, and added taxpayer protections against the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from October 1992 until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993, despite 50 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have eliminated the capital gains tax entirely, rolled individual tax rates back to a flat two-tier 15/28% structure, and ended the 'double tax' on corporate dividends by giving shareholders a credit for taxes their companies already paid. It also would have restored deductible IRAs for everyone, allowed penalty-free retirement withdrawals to buy a first home, pay college costs, or handle a medical crisis, created a credit of up to $2,500 for first-time homebuyers, and repealed excise taxes on luxury cars, boats, aircraft, jewelry, and furs. A second title created a 'Taxpayer Bill of Rights,' establishing an independent advocate inside the IRS and new protections for people facing collection, liens, and erroneous information returns.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest beneficiaries would be high-income households that realize capital gains and dividends, since the bill eliminated the capital gains tax, credited shareholders for corporate taxes paid, cut the top rate to 28%, and restored accelerated depreciation and the investment credit — with no offsetting revenue increases in the bill. Ordinary savers and would-be homebuyers would also have gained from restored IRA deductions, penalty-free withdrawals for homes, education, and medical crises, the homebuyer credit, income averaging, and stronger IRS taxpayer protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors, corporations, and retirement savers

how_it_helps.text: It would exempt all net capital gains from federal income tax, including for alternative minimum tax purposes [S2, S3].
It would give individual shareholders a credit for federal income taxes paid by the corporation distributing the dividend, effectively ending the double taxation of corporate profits [S2, S3].
It would replace the individual rate structure with two brackets — 15% and 28% — eliminating the top bracket [S2, S3].

It would restore the IRA deduction for all taxpayers with inflation adjustments, create new nondeductible tax-free retirement accounts, and allow penalty-free early withdrawals for first homes, higher education, and financially devastating medical expenses [S2, S3].
It would create a credit of up to $2,500 (10% of purchase price) for first-time homebuyers, though only for residences bought between February 1, 1992 and January 1, 1993 [S2, S3].
It would restore income averaging, letting people with a sudden spike in income spread it over three prior years for tax purposes [S2, S3].

It would establish a Taxpayer Advocate inside the IRS, require notice before changing installment agreements, allow withdrawal of liens and return of levied property, and create civil damages for fraudulent information returns filed against taxpayers [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill's tax cuts — capital gains repeal, lower top rates, the dividend credit, permanent research credit, restored investment credit and accelerated depreciation, and repeal of luxury excise taxes — came with no revenue-raising offsets, so the cost would have shown up as larger deficits or pressure for spending cuts and higher taxes on others later.

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no provisions to offset the revenue lost from its tax reductions; eliminating capital gains tax, cutting the top rate, and making the research credit permanent would each reduce federal receipts [S2, S3].

Because capital gains and dividends are earned disproportionately by higher-income households, the largest tax cuts in the bill would flow to them, while the cost of the forgone revenue is spread across everyone who relies on federal spending or bears future taxes.

The first-time homebuyer credit applied only to residences purchased between February 1, 1992 and January 1, 1993 — a window that had largely already closed by the time the bill was introduced in October 1992, making the credit largely retroactive [S3].
Repealing passive loss limitations and restoring the pre-1986 accelerated cost recovery system would reopen tax shelters that reduce taxable investment income for sophisticated investors [S2, S3].

The bill would make IRS employees personally liable for litigation costs in certain cases and expand offers-in-compromise for 'best interest' reasons, which could weaken enforcement and complicate tax collection administration [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The taxpayer-rights title was a genuinely useful set of protections for ordinary people dealing with the IRS, and versions of similar ideas later became law. But the bill's dominant Title I was a large tax cut whose biggest provisions — capital gains repeal, the dividend credit, top-rate reduction, passive loss repeal, and accelerated depreciation — concentrate their benefits on high-income investors and asset holders, with no pay-fors attached. A well-designed growth package would have sized cuts against revenue; this one did not, and its homebuyer credit was mostly retroactive. On balance, the bill's value to ordinary people was real but secondary to its value to concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, hearing, or floor vote before the 102nd Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Cox introduced the bill on October 6, 1992, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1, S5].
Fifty representatives cosponsored the bill — 49 Republicans and one Democrat — including House Republican leaders Newt Gingrich and Dick Armey [S3, S4].
No further action of any kind appears in the record: no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and future taxpayers were spared the revenue cost of the bill's tax cuts; conversely, its backers gained nothing, and ordinary taxpayers lost the prospect of the bill's IRS protections and retirement-savings provisions, which died with it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal Treasury; the bill's backers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Christopher Cox
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill packaging repeal of the capital gains tax and other tax cuts with a Taxpayer Bill of Rights [S1, S3, S5].

for.name: 49 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Gingrich, Armey, DeLay, and Crane

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it died in committee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: 49 of the bill's 50 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action on it; one Democrat, Rep. Gary Condit, cosponsored.

industries.note: The bill exempted capital gains from tax entirely, credited shareholders for corporate taxes paid on dividends, and cut the top individual rate to 28%, all flowing to households with capital income. The bill included no offsetting revenue, so the forgone receipts would be borne by future taxpayers generally [S2, S3].

Repealing passive loss limitations and restoring the pre-1986 accelerated cost recovery system would once again allow investors to shelter income with paper losses and fast depreciation deductions, a benefit largely unavailable to wage earners [S2, S3].

The bill made the research credit permanent, restored a 10% investment tax credit, and repealed luxury excise taxes on vehicles, boats, and aircraft, lowering the cost of investment for these firms at federal revenue expense [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Luxury goods makers (autos, boats, aircraft, jewelry, furs)
industries.note: The bill repealed the 1990 luxury excise taxes, whose statutory burden fell on affluent buyers of these goods; repeal would lift costs on both makers and buyers with a modest revenue loss [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Banks, brokerages, and mutual fund companies
industries.note: Restoring the universal IRA deduction and creating new tax-free retirement accounts would channel more household savings into these institutions while also benefiting the savers themselves [S2, S3].
